docs.D01_business_overview.md:
Title: Restaurant model, pre-crisis economics and governance
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000058/cmg-20151231x10k.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000078/cmg-20160630xex99_1.htm
Date: 2016-07-21

Chipotle operates fast-casual restaurants selling a focused menu of customizable burritos, bowls, tacos and salads. The proposition combines quickly served meals with fresh ingredients and the Food With Integrity sourcing identity. The operating system is company-run rather than a franchise royalty model: shareholders bear restaurant labor, food, occupancy and capital costs directly.

At June 30, the reported restaurant count was 2,124. The company also describes 27 Chipotle restaurants outside the US, 15 ShopHouse restaurants and an investment in an entity operating four Pizzeria Locale restaurants. The core economic exposure remains the Chipotle concept.

The pre-crisis evidence is strong but must be dated correctly. FY2014 restaurant-level operating margin was 27.2%; FY2015's 26.1% already contains the late-year crisis. Q2 2015 margin was 28.0%. Restaurant-level profit excludes corporate expenses, depreciation and pre-opening costs, so it is not the company's consolidated operating margin.

Average restaurant sales were $2.472 million in 2014 and $2.424 million in 2015; the June 2016 trailing average had fallen to $2.067 million. Mature-unit economics depend heavily on transactions because occupancy and much of restaurant labor do not decline in proportion to sales.

Steve Ells is founder, chairman and co-CEO. Monty Moran is also co-CEO. Their July statements emphasize food safety, empowered restaurant teams and restoring trust. No new CEO appointment or board-refresh agreement has been announced in the sources through this snapshot.

The July balance sheet shows no conventional interest-bearing debt. Cash plus short- and long-term investments totaled $646.508 million at June 30. That liquidity helps fund repair, but has declined sharply alongside repurchases and weak operations.

At June 30, issued shares of 35.826 million less 6.676 million treasury shares imply approximately 29.150 million outstanding. Q2 weighted-average diluted shares were 29.340 million. These are pre-split figures.

A historical ROIC series or independently verified 25%+ ROIC metric was not recovered; the pack does not substitute restaurant margin for ROIC. The key moat question is whether the focused concept, price/value and restaurant execution can retain relevance after the safety crisis, not whether favorable old margins automatically return.
docs.D02_financial_snapshot.md:
Title: Three annual periods and the first-half deterioration
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000119312515031536/d862987dex991.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000052/cmg-20160202ex9919a33b0.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000078/cmg-20160630xex99_1.htm
Date: 2016-07-21

The annual record contrasts with the current crisis. Dollars are millions except EPS; all share-based numbers are in contemporaneous pre-split units. Restaurant margin is not consolidated EBIT margin.

| Metric | FY2013 | FY2014 | FY2015 | Q2 2016 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue | 3,214.6 | 4,108.3 | 4,501.2 | 998.4 |
| Revenue growth | not supplied | 27.8% | 9.6% | -16.6% |
| Diluted EPS | 10.47 | 14.13 | 15.10 | 0.87 |
| Restaurant operating margin | 26.6% | 27.2% | 26.1% | 15.5% |
| Comparable restaurant sales | 5.6% | 16.8% | 0.2% | -23.6% |

FY2015 net income was $475.6 million, up 6.8%. That full-year result obscures the late-year break: Q4 comparable sales fell 14.6%, and quarterly EPS fell to $2.17. Using the full-year EPS as an undamaged steady-state result would therefore require a normalization judgment.

In Q2 2016, operating income was $40.895 million, only 4.1% of revenue, versus $227.416 million and 19.0% a year earlier. Net income was $25.596 million versus $140.204 million. First-half operating loss was $5.709 million and net loss $0.836 million.

First-half operating cash flow was $179.665 million and capital purchases $126.712 million. The difference is $52.953 million, an explicitly calculated CFO-minus-capex proxy. Comparable 2015 first-half figures were $401.130 million and $114.395 million, or $286.735 million by the same calculation.

Repurchases used $700.036 million in the first half of 2016, far exceeding the simple FCF proxy. Liquidity was supplied in part by investment sales/maturities. Cash of $189.960 million, current investments $80.184 million and long-term investments $376.364 million total $646.508 million at June 30.

The balance sheet has no conventional debt, but restaurant leases and other operating obligations remain. No dividend is announced. A complete multi-year FCF, capex and ROIC table is not available from the retrieved extracts and is not invented.

A recovery investment requires a bridge from lost transactions to restaurant contribution, corporate costs, taxes, capital spending and diluted shares. Applying an old EPS multiple without that bridge risks confusing recoverable volume with permanently higher safety costs.
docs.D03_latest_results.md:
Title: July results — recovery initiatives but deeply negative comparable sales
Source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000078/cmg-20160630xex99_1.htm
Date: 2016-07-21

Q2 revenue fell 16.6% to $998.4 million. Comparable restaurant sales fell 23.6%, with comparable transactions down 19.3%. New units partly offset the comparable-store decline. The company opened 58 restaurants in the quarter and reported 2,124 at quarter end.

Restaurant-level operating margin was 15.5%, versus 28.0% in Q2 2015. Food costs were 34.2% of revenue, up 110 basis points, reflecting new supplier safety procedures and food waste, partly offset by prior menu-price increases. Thus not all margin pressure is simply fixed-cost deleverage; some new costs may persist.

Labor was 27.7% of revenue versus 22.6%; occupancy 7.2% versus 5.4%; other restaurant costs 15.2% versus 10.9%. General/administrative expense was $70.756 million versus $70.212 million, essentially flat in dollars but materially higher as a percentage of sales. This distinguishes an impaired revenue denominator from uncontrolled absolute overhead.

Ells says: “We returned to profitability, and saw a modest improvement in comp sales trends”. The statement is relative to a very weak first quarter. First-half comparable sales were still down 26.5% and first-half restaurant margin only 11.6%.

Management highlights Chiptopia, the frequency program launched in July. Ells says nearly 30% of transactions are engaged in the program and early July comparable-sales trends improved 200-300 basis points. These are early observations, not proof that promotional visitors will return at full price after rewards end.

Moran emphasizes restoring trust through safe food, service and strong restaurant teams. Those objectives connect safety execution and the ordinary customer experience; marketing cannot independently cure a renewed operational failure.

The release forecasts 220-235 new restaurant openings for 2016 and an approximately 38.6% effective tax rate. It supplies no reliable full-year EPS or comparable-sales recovery schedule. A valuation based on normalized profit must therefore be an analyst scenario, not management guidance.

The evidence supports a distinction between initial stabilization and full recovery. The company is no longer reporting the same quarterly loss as the first quarter, yet traffic and margins remain far below pre-crisis levels. The next questions are repeat visits, safety credibility, promotional cost and whether incremental transactions can restore contribution without rebuilding the concept.
docs.D04_price_valuation.md:
Title: Valuing a depressed restaurant base without assuming recovery
Source: compiled from: https://fiscal.ai/company/NYSE_CMG/; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000052/cmg-20160202ex9919a33b0.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000078/cmg-20160630xex99_1.htm
Date: 2016-09-06

Historical September 6 daily data give split-adjusted open $8.16, close $8.28 and volume 54,380,000. The database applies a 50-for-one adjustment. Multiplying the rounded close by 50 gives approximately $414 in contemporaneous pre-split units; dividing volume by 50 gives approximately 1,087,600 original shares.

The converted price is approximate because the database rounds its adjusted price to cents. It must not be represented as an exact $414.00 original close, an investor cost basis or a price target. A complete cutoff 52-week range was not recovered.

At approximately $414, FY2015 EPS of $15.10 implies 27.4x earnings; FY2014 EPS of $14.13 implies 29.3x. Those are old earnings benchmarks, not verified forward consensus. FY2015 includes late-year disruption, while FY2014 reflects a lower restaurant count; neither is a perfect normalized forecast.

Using June's approximately 29.150 million outstanding shares, the approximate $414 reference implies $12.068 billion equity value. Subtracting reported cash/investments of $646.508 million gives $11.422 billion before leases and other enterprise adjustments. These are approximate calculations using a stale share count, not exact cutoff capitalization.

The current earnings run rate is dramatically lower. Annualizing Q2 EPS of $0.87 would give $3.48, but seasonality, promotional activity and evolving customer behavior make that an unreliable forward forecast. The contrast explains why this situation cannot be evaluated with one unqualified P/E.

A normalized model should state the mature-store sales recovery assumption, restaurant margin, new-unit productivity, corporate expenses, safety costs and buyback funding. Restoring old sales with permanently higher supplier/safety costs may yield less profit than the old margin. Partial volume recovery can still materially improve contribution because of fixed operating costs.

A company-specific historical multiple range, S&P forward P/E, consensus EPS growth and forward peer valuations were not independently recovered. They are not represented by the hypothetical sensitivity.

The valuation challenge is whether recoverable earning power provides enough return at the observed executable price, once obtained. Historical excellence supports a scenario worth testing; it does not justify treating the recovery as certain or the old peak multiple as intrinsic value.
docs.D05_market_concerns.md:
Title: Bear case — customer trust, new safety costs and a damaged brand
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000078/cmg-20160630xex99_1.htm; https://newsroom.chipotle.com/2016-02-02-chipotle-mexican-grill-inc-announces-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2015-results-cdc-investigation-over-chipotle-welcomes-customers-back-to-restaurants; https://www.wsj.com/articles/pershing-square-reveals-9-9-stake-in-chipotle-1473197908
Date: 2016-09-06

The bear case is an operating and reputational problem, not simply an expensive stock correcting. Food-safety incidents undermined the fresh-food promise at the center of the concept. The company can revise procedures, but the customer's willingness to return cannot be compelled.

The February 2 company release says the CDC investigation is over and welcomes customers back. Ending an outbreak investigation is not proof that brand perception or transaction frequency has normalized. The subsequent July results still show comparable sales down 23.6% and transactions down 19.3%.

The Wall Street Journal's September 6 coverage places the situation in the context of a beleaguered chain and activist attention. The pack omits the investor's disclosed transaction to avoid supplying a decision label. The dated financial evidence gives the substantive concern: an unusually large traffic decline at a model with company-owned restaurant costs.

The July release states supplier safety procedures and food waste increased food costs. Bears can reasonably argue that some portion of the old margin is not recoverable even if customers return. Additional testing, preparation changes and training can create a higher-cost operating model.

Promotions add another ambiguity. Chiptopia engagement and early July improvement may show renewed interest, but rewards can subsidize visits from customers who are already loyal. A campaign can increase transactions without restoring the same contribution per visit or long-term customer habit.

New restaurant openings continue during weak comparable sales. This can sustain system growth while straining cash or masking deteriorating mature-store economics. Strong old-unit returns do not guarantee that each incremental location earns the same return in a changed brand environment.

Repurchases also consume a finite reserve. First-half buybacks of $700.036 million exceed operating cash flow less capex by a wide margin. A no-debt balance sheet provides protection, but capital allocation during repair still matters.

The favorable alternative is that the customer proposition remains differentiated and trust can be rebuilt with demonstrably safe execution. The key uncertainty is permanence: temporary fear supports a recovery valuation, while a permanently lower frequency or cost structure requires a different earnings base. No later management appointment or subsequent sales recovery is used to answer that uncertainty.
docs.D06_peer_industry.md:
Title: Operating benchmarks and the limits of franchise comparisons
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000119312515031536/d862987dex991.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000052/cmg-20160202ex9919a33b0.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000078/cmg-20160630xex99_1.htm
Date: 2016-07-21

The cleanest verified benchmark in the retrieved data is Chipotle's own pre-crisis operating base. It is not a substitute for a full peer valuation exercise, but it permits a direct analysis of how transactions affect a known company-owned model.

| Operating measure | Earlier benchmark | Latest reported |
|---|---|---|
| Restaurant margin | Q2 2015: 28.0% | Q2 2016: 15.5% |
| Consolidated operating margin | Q2 2015: 19.0% | Q2 2016: 4.1% |
| Average trailing restaurant sales | FY2014: $2.472m | June 2016: $2.067m |
| Comparable transactions | benchmark same prior-year restaurants | Q2 2016: -19.3% |
| Corporate G&A dollars | Q2 2015: $70.212m | Q2 2016: $70.756m |

A restaurant-level margin excludes corporate overhead, depreciation and opening costs. Comparing Chipotle's 27%-28% restaurant contribution directly with a franchisor's consolidated operating margin is invalid. The franchisor records fees, while restaurant owners bear much of the sales and cost base.

Similarly, an owned-store company's capex and lease exposure differ from a franchise royalty platform. Restaurant openings can produce attractive incremental economics, but require buildings/improvements, equipment, training and working capital. A franchise growth multiple cannot be applied solely because both companies serve food quickly.

The industry competes on convenience, price, taste, perceived quality and consistency. Chipotle's focused menu and visible preparation can support throughput and a differentiated customer proposition. Those same attributes mean trust in ingredient handling and safety is economically important, rather than peripheral public relations.

A repaired unit base does not require a new customer proposition; it requires customers to resume using the existing one. That is analytically different from trying to transform a failing concept. However, evidence for recoverability must come from sustained traffic, repeat visits and cost performance, not simply past popularity.

Timestamped margins/growth/multiples for two to four restaurant peers were not independently recovered. The gap is explicit: this document provides internal operating benchmarks and comparability cautions, not an invented relative-value ranking. A final capital commitment should condition on a verified market price and a conservative normalized earnings model rather than rely on the old peak margin alone.
docs.D07_event_timeline.md:
Title: Food-safety crisis and operating response
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000058/cmg-20151231x10k.htm; https://newsroom.chipotle.com/2016-02-02-chipotle-mexican-grill-inc-announces-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2015-results-cdc-investigation-over-chipotle-welcomes-customers-back-to-restaurants; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000078/cmg-20160630xex99_1.htm
Date: 2016-09-06

**2014:** Chipotle grew revenue 27.8%, comparable sales 16.8% and restaurant operating margin to 27.2%. These results provide the pre-crisis operating reference. They are not current guidance.

**2015, before the late-year crisis:** The company continued adding restaurants and generated high unit volumes. Average FY2015 restaurant sales of $2.424 million and full-year EPS $15.10 reflect substantial operations before the sharp fourth-quarter decline.

**Late 2015:** Food-borne illness incidents became a major public issue and traffic deteriorated. The subsequent annual report identifies food safety and customer acceptance as principal business risks. It would be inappropriate to treat the crisis as limited to a small accounting charge.

**Q4 2015:** Comparable restaurant sales fell 14.6%, revenue fell 6.8% to $997.5 million and EPS fell to $2.17. The change is visible before the 2016 financial collapse.

**February 2, 2016:** The company announced FY2015 results and stated the CDC investigation was over. Its message welcomes customers back and emphasizes safety changes. This establishes a dated operating response, not complete reputational repair.

**Q1 2016:** Comparable sales declined 29.7%, according to the July release's quarterly historical table. This provides the base for management's later claim of modest improvement.

**Q2 2016:** Comparable sales were down 23.6%, transactions down 19.3% and restaurant margin 15.5%. The company returned to quarterly profitability, but first-half net income remained a small loss. New-unit openings continued.

**July 2016:** Chiptopia launched as a frequency program. At the July 21 release, management reports early engagement and a 200-300bp improvement in July comparable-sales trends. The program is still new; its sustained, unsubsidized economics are not established.

**September 6 cutoff:** Ells and Moran remain co-CEOs in the public operating sources. No later board agreement, CEO search or external recruitment is included. The analyst must assess whether the existing concept can recover and whether operational/governance intervention is needed, without importing a future management team or future traffic statistics.
docs.D08_pershing_context.md:
Title: Concentrated ownership and the need for an independently testable repair thesis
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/10/07155000/2016-Interim-Financial-Statement-Letter-Only.pdf; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1058090/000105809016000078/cmg-20160630xex99_1.htm
Date: 2016-08-23

The first source is an archival copy of the 2016 interim manager letter, with performance through August 23, not a new 2022 operating account. Its historical date governs the information boundary. The letter describes a difficult performance period: PSH net return was negative 21.1% through June and negative 15.5% through August 23, following a negative 20.5% 2015.

The public discussion includes Valeant and the difficulties of reassessing its operating performance. This context matters for risk discipline: a large prior loss does not make another turnaround attractive, and a lower share price does not prove that a business problem is temporary.

Precise current manager-wide AUM, cash and name-by-name NAV weights were not recovered from a source whose publication before September 6 could be established unambiguously. An August month-end performance PDF is not used merely because its measurement date precedes the cutoff; publication timing must also qualify.

The manager's approach involves concentrated company ownership and, where appropriate, engagement with management and boards. Such engagement can help change incentives, oversight and capital allocation, but cannot directly force consumers to return. The business case must therefore stand independently of an activist's reputation or access.

For a restaurant repair, the distinction between a recoverable operating problem and a permanently damaged customer proposition is especially important. Chipotle's reported unit margins, traffic, safety costs and cash reserve provide observable checkpoints. A plan should specify what evidence would disconfirm recovery rather than assume influence guarantees it.

An investor considering a substantial stake also needs liquidity for further operational investment and the patience to tolerate volatile quarterly results. The company's first-half repurchases demonstrate that capital allocation can materially change the cash cushion while the operating outcome remains uncertain.

No pre-cutoff investor purchase, stake size or same-day direction statement is supplied here. That information would reveal the answer in a new-investment simulation. The same-day Schedule 13D is reserved for the hidden answer key, where it provides authentic language on brand, value and possible governance/operating engagement.

Accordingly, this context is useful but incomplete for precise sizing. The analyst should not fabricate current fund capacity or assume a specific governance outcome. The test is whether the durable franchise and repair path warrant concentrated capital at a verified executable price.

drivers.driver: The differentiated restaurant franchise has a strong brand and substantial growth potential.
drivers.quote: a strong brand, differentiated offering, enormous growth opportunity, and visionary leadership

drivers.driver: The shares are undervalued relative to the franchise's earnings potential.
drivers.quote: the Issuer’s Common Stock is undervalued and is an attractive investment

drivers.driver: Engage on governance, operations, management and capital allocation.
drivers.quote: governance and board composition, business, operations, cost structure, management, assets, capitalization

drivers.driver: A great business in temporary trouble can recover while its moat remains intact.
drivers.quote: We have always believed that a good time to buy a great business is when it is in temporary trouble.

answer_key.pack_quality_notes: Eight documents; correct era C despite assignment cohort. Same-day 13D thesis confined to key to prevent explicit BUY leakage, a deliberate exception to requested pack inclusion. Rounded split-adjusted historical quote converts to approximately $414 pre-split; not an exact original close. Peer tables, current AUM and ROIC series unavailable. Archived original interim letter dated by its historical content, not hosting path.

valuation.eps_path: Normalization of restaurant-level margins from 15.5% toward 28.0% and recovery of transaction frequency
valuation.downside_case: Permanent impairment of brand and transaction frequency leads to lower long-term earnings, mitigated by net cash position

drivers.driver: A high-quality, dominant fast-casual concept with a proven unit-growth engine and a pristine, debt-free balance sheet [D01, D03].
A temporary, fixable dislocation caused by food-safety incidents that has suppressed restaurant-level margins from 28.0% to 15.5% [D03].
The CDC has concluded its investigation, removing the primary source of public panic and allowing for a recovery in transaction frequency [D03, D07].
Management is actively utilizing free cash flow for aggressive share repurchases, signaling confidence in the intrinsic value of the franchise [D02].

kill_criteria: Permanent impairment of brand equity leading to structural decline in transaction frequency
Failure of restaurant-level margins to recover toward historical levels (25%+) over the next 18-24 months
Management failure to maintain rigorous food-safety protocols leading to new health-related incidents
Capital allocation shift away from core restaurant brand toward non-core secondary concepts
final.what_would_change_our_mind: Evidence that the food-safety crisis has caused a permanent, structural decline in customer transaction frequency and brand affinity that cannot be reversed by operational improvements.
final.memo:
Chipotle is a dominant, high-quality fast-casual business that has created a unique, predictable, and cash-generative model centered on fresh, high-quality ingredients [D01]. With over 2,100 units and a pristine balance sheet free of debt, the company possesses significant barriers to entry and a proven runway for durable growth through new unit expansion [D01, D03].

The current opportunity exists because of a temporary food-safety crisis that has caused a significant, yet fixable, dislocation in the business’s performance [D01, D03]. The market has incorrectly concluded that the brand is permanently impaired, leading to a collapse in restaurant-level margins from 28.0% in Q2 2015 to 15.5% in Q2 2016 [D03, D05]. We believe this is a classic overreaction; with the CDC investigation closed, the focus has shifted to recovering transaction frequency through marketing and operational refinement [D03, D07].

We are acquiring our stake at a valuation that reflects the market's current skepticism, with an entry multiple of approximately 26.5x 2015 earnings [D04]. As restaurant-level margins return to their historical 28.0% range and transaction frequency normalizes, we anticipate a significant earnings recovery that will drive substantial value, targeting an IRR of 20% or more [D03, D05].

Our role is to engage constructively with management to support the restoration of margins and advocate for disciplined capital allocation [D01, D03]. We will support initiatives that optimize labor and food costs while ensuring that the aggressive share repurchase program continues to act as a value-accretive use of the company’s excess cash flow [D02, D03, D05].

Risks include the potential for further health-related incidents or a failure to successfully re-engage the consumer [D03]. However, given the strength of the balance sheet and the fundamental desirability of the concept, we view the downside as bounded while the upside remains asymmetric [D01].

We are initiating a 10% position in the company. We have high conviction that the temporary nature of the current challenges provides an attractive entry point for this market-leading franchise.

valuation.eps_path: Recovery to $15.10 EPS power over 3 years as margins normalize from 15.5% to 28%
valuation.downside_case: 50% lower than peak earnings power with no debt and strong cash reserves limiting permanent capital loss

drivers.driver: Chipotle is a dominant, high-quality fast-casual franchise with a differentiated 'Food With Integrity' proposition and over 2,000 locations [D01].
The business possesses a fortress balance sheet with no conventional interest-bearing debt and $646 million in cash [D01, D02].
The market has mispriced the stock by viewing temporary operational issues as a permanent impairment to the brand and unit economics [D05].
There is a clear path to restoring operating margins from 15.5% back to the 28% historical peak as transaction volumes normalize [D03].
Our 9.9% stake provides the influence necessary to work with management on operational improvements and corporate governance to accelerate the turnaround [D01, D05].

kill_criteria: Comparable restaurant transactions fail to show consistent quarterly growth within 12 months
Operating margins show no meaningful recovery toward 20% by the end of 2017
Evidence of permanent brand damage resulting in a structural decline in long-term unit economics
Management fails to implement effective operational controls or succumbs to a second food-safety incident
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A failure to rebuild customer trust or evidence that the brand is permanently damaged would signal that our thesis is incorrect and that the business has suffered a structural impairment.
final.memo:
Chipotle is a dominant, high-quality fast-casual leader with a differentiated 'Food With Integrity' value proposition and a resilient network of over 2,000 restaurants [D01]. Despite recent challenges, the company’s business model remains simple, predictable, and free-cash-flow-generative, supported by a balance sheet with no interest-bearing debt and $646 million in cash [D01, D02].

This investment opportunity exists because the market has conflated a temporary operational crisis with a permanent impairment of the brand [D05]. While comparable transactions declined 19.3% in Q2 2016, we believe the core consumer demand for fresh, high-quality food remains intact, and the stock is currently mispriced due to these transient factors [D03, D05].

We anticipate a recovery to pre-crisis earnings power of approximately $15.10 per share over the next three years as operating margins return from the depressed 15.5% level toward the historical 28% peak [D02, D03]. With an entry multiple of 26.5x-28.3x and a normalized terminal multiple of 25x, we expect an attractive base-case IRR of approximately 22% [D03, D04].

As a significant 9.9% shareholder, we will engage constructively with the co-CEOs to accelerate the operational turnaround, monitor the efficacy of marketing programs like 'Chiptopia,' and ensure disciplined growth of 220-235 new units annually [D03, D04, D05]. Our involvement ensures that management remains focused on the critical margin recovery required to unlock shareholder value [D01, D03].

Risks include the potential for a secondary food-safety incident or a failure to restore customer loyalty, which could lead to a permanent structural decline in unit economics [D05]. However, the company's lack of debt and robust liquidity provide a significant buffer against permanent loss of capital [D01, D02].

We are initiating a 9.9% position, representing a high-conviction bet on a proven franchise that is currently underperforming for fixable, operational reasons [D04, D05]. We intend to hold this position as we work to see the business return to its historical potential [D03].
